extracted.intended_audience: mathematics department faculty, course instructors, and departmental assessment coordinators at colleges and universities
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, running, and using course portfolios, placement tests, and other departmental assessment initiatives in undergraduate mathematics departments. Covers portfolio construction, evidence selection, placement-test design and logistics, data analysis, and uses of findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek agreement about portfolio purposes and ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek agreement at the outset about the purposes of portfolios, who will use the information, who owns it, what's at stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify stakeholders, intended uses (e.g., internal improvement, peer review, external evaluation), and ownership/confidentiality before compiling materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be selective in evidence collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Be selective. The power of the portfolio comes from sampling performance, not amassing every possible scrap of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose representative, high-quality samples rather than collecting all artifacts; curate to make a convincing case without overwhelming readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the portfolio as an argument or thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of the portfolio as an argument, a case, a thesis with relevant evidence and examples cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure materials to support specific claims about teaching and learning; include evidence that directly ties to stated claims/goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize the portfolio around goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the portfolio around goals, your own goals or departmental goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make goals explicit (course-level or departmental). Use goals to select evidence and to frame reflective commentary and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a variety of evidence from multiple sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a variety of kinds of evidence from a variety of sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine classroom assessments, homework samples, exams, projects, peer observations, and student feedback to provide multiple perspectives on learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reflective commentary on evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide reflective commentary on evidence. Reflective commentary is useful in revealing the pedagogical thinking behind various kinds of evidence and helping readers to know what to look for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why each piece of evidence was chosen, what it shows about student learning, and how it influenced instructional decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment with formats and refine portfolios
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with various formats and structures, be deliberate about whether portfolios are working and how you can refine the structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try different organizational schemes or presentation formats and iterate based on feedback and effectiveness for intended audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include syllabus to show coverage vs intent
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be useful to include the actual course syllabus, to show what the instructor actually covered in the course in comparison with what the instructor intended to cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide syllabus alongside evidence so readers can assess alignment between intended curriculum and what was taught/assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use focused portfolios when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A variant is the 'focused portfolio,' which concentrates on one specific aspect or goal of a mathematics course and the progress made toward the goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on a single measurable goal (e.g., integration of graphing calculators, transition to proof-writing) and collect targeted evidence of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a cover letter or preface explaining purpose and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a cover letter or preface to the reader, briefly explaining the purpose and methods of the portfolio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize goals, selection criteria, assessment methods, and intended audience at the front to orient reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the student voice
rubrics_metrics.description: An important addition to the portfolio is the 'student voice,' so the portfolio clearly represents not only what the instructor saw in the course, but also what the students got out of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include informal class assessments, formal student evaluations, surveys, and samples of student homework and projects to reflect students' perspectives and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use portfolios as course records and guides for successive instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: One immediate benefit of the portfolio is a course record. A course portfolio would give that faculty member a sense of coverage, the level of sophistication in presenting the material, and standards of achievement. The course portfolio also gives a platform for successive development of a course by several faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain portfolios as living documents to hand off to other instructors and to document curricular continuity and changes across terms and instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design portfolios to support external peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a course portfolio presents the possibility of using the material for external evaluation. Peers are essential for feedback in teaching because they are the most familiar with the content on a substantive level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare portfolios with clear evidence and commentary to facilitate peer review; identify what peers should inspect and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use assessments to diagnose specific student-learning strengths and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use classroom assessments, background probes, exams and final exams to document where students learned key topics acceptably and where they had more trouble (example: modeling and linear programming OK; queuing and dynamic programming weaker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze assessment results to detect patterns (e.g., topics mastered vs. problematic areas) and use findings to plan targeted instructional changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek agreement and dialogue with client disciplines about needed quantitative skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask teachers in other disciplines for a practical set of specific quantitative knowledge that will be essential in science courses; pre-tests are designed and results are used for discussions with students, mathematics faculty, and client disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaboratively define outcome expectations with client departments and use shared assessments/pre-tests to align coursework with those needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pre-/post-testing and mixed assessment methods for curriculum reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs stress breadth, from pre- and post-testing, to journals, comparative test questions, interviews of students, end of semester attitudinal questionnaires, and more. Good assessment is an interaction between formative and summative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ both formative measures (e.g., journals, in-class probes) and summative measures (pre/post-tests, exams) and triangulate to inform reforms and measure effects over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer multiple targeted placement tests over a single test
rubrics_metrics.description: The one placement test evolved into three separate tests; one major realization was the inadequacy of a single test for accurate placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design separate placement instruments for clearly different student populations/backgrounds (e.g., basic arithmetic, algebra/trig, calculus-ready) to improve placement accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect contextual questionnaire data with placement tests
rubrics_metrics.description: All three exams contain an initial list of subjective questions asking students for information about (1) their motivation for taking mathematics; (2) the number of terms of mathematics they plan to take; (3) the area in which they expect to major; (4) what their last mathematics course was, and their grade in this course; and (5) how extensively they have used calculators. Questions on the regular and advanced exams also ask for (6) how much trigonometry and calculus they have had; and (7) the mathematics course in which they think they should enroll.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-reported background and intention items to augment test scores and to detect misplacements or cases needing advisor intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define clear timed-exam and calculator policies
rubrics_metrics.description: The exams all are timed exams with a ninety minute limit. Students taking the Advanced and Regular Exams are allowed to use calculators without a QWERTY keyboard. Currently, students are not allowed to use calculators on the Basic Exam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set and communicate consistent timing and calculator rules aligned to the constructs being measured; enforce restrictions to maintain test security and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design placement exams to match audience and topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Three exams: Advanced (locally written first-semester calculus section + MAA trig/functions), Regular (trig/functions + MAA calculator-based algebra), Basic (MAA arithmetic/basic skills + MAA algebra). Each test targets a different audience and has specific question counts and topic coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose each placement instrument with content and item types appropriate to the target placement decisions; document topic breakdowns for advising use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine test scores with admissions and background data via regression to predict success
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement recommendations are computed using a large number of regression equations combining admissions information and placement test scores to predict gradepoints as the quantifiable measure of successful placement. There are regression equations for 24 cases, used in five different sets depending on available information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistical models (e.g., regression) that incorporate test scores, prior achievement, and background variables to predict likely course grades and to set placement cutoffs; refine models over time using historical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cutoff programs but review borderline and special cases separately
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer assigns a recommendation to each student using a cutoff program that is refined from year to year. Borderline and special cases (e.g., low class rank from a selective high school) are considered separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automate routine placements but build in human review for outliers, borderline scores, and documented special circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide individual counseling and advisor notification after testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the exams...I counsel students who have questions about their placement recommendation; notify instructors of students in their classes who did not take an examination or who did not follow the placement recommendation; and assist students with changes among calculus sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure a process for students to appeal/counsel and that advisors/instructors receive placement information promptly to support appropriate enrollment and interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use explicit score thresholds for honors/regular placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, students with gr scores of 3.5 or above are given a recommendation for honors Calculus I; those with scores between 3.3 and 3.5 are told they may make their own choice between the honors and regular versions of Calculus I; and those with scores below 3.3 are given a recommendation for regular Calculus I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set transparent numeric cutoffs tied to predicted grade models to guide placement into differentiated course versions; communicate policy to students and faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign a dedicated coordinator/director for placement programs
rubrics_metrics.description: The current St. Olaf mathematics placement program is administered by a member of the mathematics faculty who is given a half course teaching credit for serving as director. The Director sends each new student a letter early in the summer...manages details of giving the exams and reporting the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide named responsibility (with workload credit) to oversee logistics, communications, data analysis, and counseling associated with the placement program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure placement program success with outcome metrics and refine
rubrics_metrics.description: The success and efficiency of this placement process...is rewarded by the number of students who successfully complete their initial courses in mathematics. In the first semesters...92% of the students who initially enrolled in a calculus course completed a semester of calculus; and of these, 92% received a grade of C– or above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track outcomes such as course completion rates and distribution of grades for assessed placements; use these metrics to validate and refine placement models and cutoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement mandatory, large-scale readiness testing with advising integration
rubrics_metrics.description: By 1988, the MRT program was fully implemented for all new students enrolling in courses from intermediate algebra to Calculus I. Over 5,000 students participate each year. Summer orientation sessions provide testing, advising, and registration; results are distributed before advising so advisors can help students select appropriate courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate testing into orientation/advising workflows, make testing mandatory where appropriate, and ensure timely distribution of results to enable informed registration decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide detailed student profiles and topic breakdowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Each student receives a profile sheet indicating their mathematics placement and a breakdown of their total score by topic. (Questions are grouped into 7–8 topic areas, such as linear functions, simplifying expressions, and solving equations.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver breakdowns to students and advisors so they understand strengths/weaknesses by topic and can make informed course choices or remediation plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block registration into higher-level courses and allow advisor overrides
rubrics_metrics.description: The computerized registration process blocks students from registering for courses at a higher level. The coordinator makes final decisions when overriding any initial placement based on test results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use system controls to prevent misregistration above recommended levels while allowing qualified, reviewed overrides via advisors/coordinator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative placement evidence for some students
rubrics_metrics.description: One of these is the high school GPA which is automatically considered for freshmen whose scores fall near a cut-off. A pilot placement program began allowing freshmen to place into calculus based on high PSAT or ACT mathematics scores without taking Test B. Transfer students are allowed to use prerequisite coursework in addition to their test results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate validated alternative indicators (standardized test scores, prior coursework, GPA) for borderline cases or as alternate pathways to placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit test retakes and manage appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, the same test cannot be taken more than once within any three-month period. This has lowered the number of appeals from students claiming, 'I just forgot the material...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set retake policies to deter gaming, and document appeals procedures; offer legitimate retake opportunities under controlled conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuously monitor, analyze, and adjust placement procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of each year, an analysis is made of the success of the various placement procedures. Adjustments may be made and monitored during the following semester.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly analyze placement distributions and outcomes, refine regression models/cutoffs, and implement operational changes iteratively.
